subtitulo: Master's thesis · nonlinear simulation with ANSYS
resumen: Nonlinear simulation of an M12×1.5 bolted joint in tension: materials, boundary conditions, mesh sensitivity, nine cases and a comparison with a 3D helical model.

puntos: See how the relative nut strength R and the friction coefficient μ change the behaviour of the joint.
Estimate the failure mode of the joint.
Check whether the analytical predictions and published theory are actually reflected in the simulated joint.

bloques.titulo: From a field problem to a parametric study
parrafos: I wrote this thesis for the master’s in Industrial Engineering at UPC (ETSEIB) during an exchange at the Department of Mechanical Engineering of the Universidad de Santiago de Chile (USACH).

The starting point was a USACH study of wheel-loss incidents in mining vehicles. Tensile test data were available for the joints and bolt specimens. The measured response included the compliance of the machine and grips, and the actual geometry, nut properties and friction were undocumented.

I set up a parametric numerical tensile test on an M12×1.5 joint with modelled threads. In ANSYS I combined frictional contact between flanks, plasticity and large deflection, and ran three relative nut strengths R against three friction coefficients μ.

bloques.titulo: Materials · from test data to a plasticity model
parrafos: I started from testing-machine force readings and video-based diameter measurements of specimens machined from the bolt core. The video could not resolve the elastic range. No tensile tests of the nuts were available, and the hardness readings were not enough to build a nut curve.

I corrected the video scale using the initial area inferred from peak force and measured tensile strength. I excluded invalid specimens and pre-peak readings, applied the Bridgman correction during necking and subtracted elastic strain. This yielded 13 usable points from three specimens, spanning 0.052 to 0.939 plastic strain.

I compared the Hollomon and Ludwik laws and selected Ludwik with an assumed 900 MPa yield stress, checked against the specimens’ ultimate tensile strength. I scaled the stresses for the nuts while keeping E and ν fixed. The three ANSYS tables contain 22 true stress–plastic strain pairs each.

I extended the law to εp = 2.1. When the table runs out, ANSYS uses perfect plasticity. In early runs the loss of tangent stiffness increased iterations and triggered bisections in small regions beyond the experimental range. The extension maintains hardening there and is marked as a numerical extrapolation.

The axisymmetric study uses quadratic PLANE183 elements. I used mapped quadrilateral meshing in the thread engagement bands and their transitions. I refined the roots and flanks, where gradients are steepest, and used larger elements in the core, plain shank and nut body.
I compared three mesh densities at the two strength extremes. A common mesh lets me compare the nine cases at the same discretisation level.
The study uses an axisymmetric section with annular threads. A monotonic axial tensile load is applied without preload. Displacement control captures the response both before and after peak force.

bloques.titulo: Local results and failure mode study
parrafos: I studied the critical locations where the different failure modes appear, and how varying the parameters affects the local response of the joint.

bloques.titulo: Evidence of failure by shank necking and nut thread shear
parrafos: Analysing the results, I found evidence of two different failure modes, which depend on the relative strength of the nut.

With a weak nut (R = 0.45) the engaged threads are the weakest link: they give way in shear and bending, starting with the first one, and the nut expands radially. With stronger nuts (R = 0.70 and 1.00) the engagement holds and deformation concentrates in the unengaged threads of the bolt, which neck until the shank reaches its limit.

The real thread is a helix. Because of limited computing capacity, I ran the parametric study with a 2D axisymmetric model, far cheaper than the 3D helical one. Finally, I ran one simulation with the 3D helical model to compare them and estimate the error introduced by simplifying the geometry.

The 2D model keeps the thread profile, flank contact and radial expansion of the nut, but loses the circumferential variation and the torsional coupling of the helix. With a helix every cross-section has the same area. With annular threads, it depends on whether the cut passes through a crest or a root.

bloques.titulo: Stress and strain in the section
bloques.intro: I compare the two models on the front section plane at four stages of the same case (R = 1.00, μ = 0.15), identified by axial displacement. The force–displacement curve marks each stage. It is a single case and does not validate the rest of the matrix.

pasos.texto: Force grows almost in proportion to displacement. Between 0.03 and 0.06 mm the secant stiffness of the 3D model is 5.04% lower than the 2D one.
The curve loses slope as the material yields. Both models follow close paths, with the 3D model slightly higher from about 0.17 mm.
Both models peak at 0.705 mm: 91.95 kN in 2D and 92.73 kN in 3D, a 0.85% difference.

At 1.2 mm the force has dropped to 90.64 kN in 2D and 91.55 kN in 3D. With stronger nuts, strain concentrates in the unengaged threads of the bolt and reduces its cross-section. The contour plots show 1.155 mm in 2D and 1.163 mm in 3D, on the same scale.

items.titulo: Nut strength decides the failure mode
items.texto: At R = 0.45 the nut threads give way by shear and bending, starting with the first one, at 66–68 kN. At R = 0.70 and 1.00 the bolt necks in its unengaged threads and the peak is about 92 kN.
Reducing μ from 0.20 to 0.10 lowers the peak by 2.6 % with the weak nut and by 0.3 % at most in the other cases. Higher friction reduces nut expansion at the same load.

items.titulo: Theory holds up in the simulation
items.texto: The analytical calculation of each mechanism ranks the failure modes in the same order as the simulations, and friction acts in the direction predicted by flank force equilibrium.

items.titulo: The 2D model captures the global response
items.texto: In the compared case, the 3D model gives a 0.85 % higher peak and a 5.04 % lower initial secant stiffness. It is a single case and local differences are larger.

bloques.nota: Numerical study with no damage model or experimental validation: the loads are plastic collapse loads, not fracture loads. Homogeneous material, no preload or cyclic loading.

items.texto: A structured helical mesh to assess load sharing between threads, shear bands and local plasticity.
Backed by tests that characterise the material, above all its shear ductility, to predict fracture and thread stripping.
Account for the surface of real bolts and nuts being harder than the core.
The closest to real service: wheel studs removed from vehicles show fatigue and bending fractures.

bloques.intro: I directed the AI-assisted development of these tools: I set the requirements, reviewed each iteration and checked the results against physical and numerical criteria.

items.texto: They set up the models, contacts, mesh, loading and solver controls.
An input file reader checks the set-up before each solution is launched.
Keeps the global load history and exports detailed fields only for the key states.
I split bounded tasks between the two assistants, with shared context and cross-review.

titulo_completo: Finite element simulation of an M12×1.5 bolt–nut joint under tension: effect of relative strength and friction on the collapse mechanism
